quote: This required neurons to maintain a certain degree of quantum coherence, which was something you could look for, and find or not find.
content: The essay's complaint is about the thirty years, not the verdict: "it would have been acceptable for me to spend thirty years on my silly idea, so long as I succeeded in falsifying it eventually." Tegmark's calculation appeared in 2000, and the hypothesis did not die. Its proponents replied, and the Orch-OR programme continues a quarter-century later (Tegmark 2000). Traditional Rationality let its adherents hold the idea until the test and keep it afterward, which is the leniency the essay describes. A Bayesian filter would have discounted the idea before the test, because it predicted nothing about neurons that anyone did not already know.

quote: Do not attempt long chains of reasoning or complicated plans.
content: The advice has a qualifying clause: complex reasoning works "only when every step is pinned down overwhelmingly." Where that is not possible, the essay's standard implies wide uncertainty. The AI-risk case in its sharpest form asks for exactly that: we do not know that superhuman systems will be safe, the stakes are large, and no long chain is needed to conclude that the question deserves work. That argument is short. The detailed scenarios the note has in mind are where the advice should bite, and the sequence's own treatment of futurists' detail, in Burdensome Details, applies it to them.

quote: if a hypothesis does not today have a favorable likelihood ratio over “I don’t know,”
content: "I don't know" is a broad predictive distribution. A hypothesis beats it only by assigning the observed data more probability than the broad distribution does, that is, by having predicted what was seen. A hypothesis that merely permits the data, as quantum-gravity neurons permitted every known fact about the brain, has a likelihood ratio of one against ignorance and gains nothing. That is what the criterion excludes, and it is what it excluded in the young Eliezer's case: "my hypothesis made no retrospective predictions." The catch-all problem arises when you need the likelihood of every unconsidered alternative. The essay needs only a comparison with a spread-out prior, and that comparison is well defined.

quote: Traditional Rationality doesn’t have the ideal that thinking is an exact art in which there is only one correct probability estimate given the evidence.
content: The essay calls it an ideal, and the Bayesian tradition supplies ways of approaching it. Objective Bayesians from Jeffreys and Jaynes onward defend priors fixed by symmetry and maximum entropy, and uniqueness has able defenders (White 2005). Even the subjectivists deliver it in the limit: agents whose priors agree about what is possible will find their posteriors merging as evidence accumulates (Blackwell & Dubins 1962). Traditional Rationality has no comparable theorem saying that disagreement must shrink. That asymmetry is the one the essay draws.
